rash.definition: acting or done without careful thought about possible consequences
sentences: The investor made a rash decision to sell all his shares in a panic, ignoring the advice of every financial analyst he consulted.
Her rash remark during the negotiation offended the delegates, and she spent the following week trying to repair the damage she had caused.
rash.mnemonic: Rash = éruption : on agit sur un coup de tête, sans réfléchir.

hasty.definition: done with excessive speed, often producing careless results
sentences: Because the committee reached a hasty verdict after only ten minutes, several members later admitted that they had overlooked crucial evidence in the case.
The editor regretted her hasty revisions, since the rushed changes introduced more errors into the manuscript than they had removed from it.
hasty.mnemonic: Hasty ressemble à haste/hâte : fait trop vite.

bleak.definition: bare and desolate; offering no hope or cheerful prospect
sentences: The bleak, windswept moor stretched endlessly before the travelers, without a single tree or building to break the gray monotony of the horizon.
With factories closing and unemployment rising, economists painted a bleak picture of the region's future, seeing little reason for any optimism at all.

grim.definition: serious and gloomy; harsh and forbidding in manner or reality
sentences: The doctor delivered the grim news that the disease had spread, and the family sat in stunned silence for several long minutes.
Rescuers faced the grim task of searching the rubble for survivors, knowing that each passing hour made a happy outcome less likely.

sullen.definition: bad-tempered and silent, showing resentful ill humor
sentences: After losing the argument, the sullen teenager slumped in the back seat and refused to answer any of his parents' friendly questions.
The sullen clerk grunted at each customer without looking up, which quickly drove away patrons who had once enjoyed the cheerful old shop.
sullen.mnemonic: Sullen : sol-itaire et boudeur, il reste dans son coin.

dirge.definition: a slow, mournful song or piece of music played at a funeral
sentences: As the coffin was lowered into the ground, the band played a solemn dirge that brought many of the mourners to tears.
The critic compared the symphony's final movement to a dirge, noting that its slow, heavy rhythms evoked loss rather than any triumphant celebration.

maudlin.definition: tearfully and foolishly sentimental, often because of drinking
sentences: After three glasses of wine, the usually reserved professor grew maudlin and began weeping over the memory of his childhood dog.
Critics dismissed the film as maudlin, complaining that its relentless appeals to the audience's emotions felt manipulative rather than genuinely touching.
maudlin.mnemonic: Maudlin vient de Madeleine (Marie-Madeleine en pleurs).

mawkish.definition: sentimental in a weak, sickly and embarrassing way
sentences: The greeting card's mawkish verse, full of syrupy promises of eternal devotion, made the recipient wince rather than smile.
Although the novelist could write moving scenes, her later books grew mawkish, drowning interesting characters in excessive and unconvincing sentimentality.

cloying.definition: disgusting or unpleasant because of excessive sweetness or sentimentality
sentences: The dessert was so cloying that after two bites I pushed the plate away, craving something sharp and bitter instead.
Many viewers found the sitcom's cloying sentimentality hard to bear, since every episode ended with the same sugary lesson about friendship.

aghast.definition: filled with shock and horror by something seen or heard
sentences: The villagers stood aghast as the flood swept away their homes, unable to speak or move in the face of such devastation.
She was aghast at the size of the bill, since the repairs had cost ten times what the mechanic had originally promised.

appall.definition: to shock and fill someone with horror or deep dismay
sentences: The graphic photographs of the disaster zone were meant to appall the public and finally push the government into taking decisive action.
Reports of the factory's dangerous conditions appalled investors, who immediately demanded that the company explain why it had ignored safety inspectors for years.

dismay.definition: a feeling of distress and worry caused by something unexpected and unwelcome
sentences: To the dismay of the organizers, heavy rain began falling an hour before the outdoor concert, leaving thousands of ticket holders huddled under umbrellas.
The board expressed dismay at the sudden resignation of the director, fearing that the unexpected departure would unsettle both employees and clients.

jarring.definition: harshly clashing and unpleasant, causing a shock to the senses
sentences: The jarring blare of the car alarm shattered the peaceful morning and made everyone on the quiet street wince.
Critics found the sudden shift from a tender love story to graphic violence jarring, since the two tones seemed completely incompatible.

humdrum.definition: lacking excitement or variety; dull and repetitive
sentences: Tired of her humdrum office routine, with the same meetings and reports every single day, she quit to travel across Asia.
The memoir transforms an otherwise humdrum life of commuting and paperwork into a fascinating story through its author's sharp wit and keen observation.
humdrum.mnemonic: Hum-drum : le bourdonnement monotone d'un tambour toujours pareil.

sentences: Copying thousands of figures by hand into the ledger was a tedious chore that left the accountant yawning long before lunch.
The lecture grew so tedious, with endless digressions and repeated examples, that half of the students quietly began checking their phones.
tedious.mnemonic: Tedious : tédieux ressemble à ennuyeux, mais pas faux ami.

tiresome.definition: causing weariness or annoyance because of being dull or repetitive
sentences: His tiresome habit of interrupting every conversation with a long personal anecdote eventually made his colleagues avoid him at lunch.
The senator found the constant press questions about the old scandal tiresome, and she answered each one with visible and growing irritation.

vapid.definition: lacking liveliness, flavor or interesting ideas; dull and insipid
sentences: The talk show host filled the hour with vapid chatter about celebrities, offering viewers not a single thoughtful or memorable idea.
Critics called the film vapid, noting that its stunning visuals could not disguise a plot with no depth and dialogue with no wit.
vapid.mnemonic: Vapid ~ vapeur : de la vapeur, rien de consistant dedans.

trite.definition: made dull and unoriginal by overuse; commonplace
sentences: The speaker's advice to 'follow your dreams' sounded trite to the graduates, who had heard the same phrase at countless ceremonies.
Although the poem began with promise, its trite rhymes about love and roses made it indistinguishable from thousands of greeting-card verses.

hackneyed.definition: lacking freshness because of having been used too often
sentences: The detective novel relied on hackneyed devices, such as the butler who did it, so no reader was surprised by the ending.
Her essay was weakened by hackneyed phrases like 'at the end of the day', which made the argument sound tired and unoriginal.
hackneyed.mnemonic: Hackney : chevaux de louage fatigués, comme des expressions usées.

trope.definition: a recurring theme, device or cliché in a genre or work of art
sentences: The lone hero who rejects society is a familiar trope in Westerns, appearing in countless films across several generations of moviemaking.
Scholars of rhetoric study the trope of the noble savage, tracing how writers repeatedly used the image to criticize their own civilization.

lackluster.definition: lacking brilliance, energy or excitement; dull
sentences: The team delivered a lackluster performance in the final, playing without energy and failing to create a single real scoring chance.
Despite the lavish advertising campaign, the product's lackluster sales disappointed shareholders, who had expected the launch to be a spectacular triumph.

staid.definition: sedate, serious and unadventurous, often in an old-fashioned way
sentences: The staid old bank, with its dark wood paneling and formal dress code, resisted every trend toward casual or experimental business practices.
Her staid parents were shocked when she dyed her hair bright green, since the family had always valued quiet respectability above all else.

riveting.definition: completely engrossing; holding one's attention firmly
sentences: The lecturer gave a riveting account of the expedition, and not one member of the audience glanced at a watch during the whole hour.
Critics praised the documentary as riveting, noting that its suspenseful structure kept viewers glued to their seats from the first scene to the last.

gripping.definition: holding attention through excitement or suspense
sentences: The author's gripping thriller kept me awake until dawn, since I simply could not put the book down before learning who the killer was.
Audiences described the courtroom drama as gripping, praising the way every scene raised the tension until the shocking final verdict.

enthrall.definition: to capture and hold the complete attention of, as if by magic
sentences: The storyteller managed to enthrall the children for hours, and they sat motionless as she described dragons, castles and hidden treasure.
Audiences were enthralled by the young pianist, whose dazzling technique and emotional depth held the entire concert hall in rapt silence.
enthrall.mnemonic: En-thrall : thrall = esclave ; on devient esclave du charme.

engross.definition: to absorb all of someone's attention or interest
sentences: The mystery novel began to engross her so completely that she missed her train stop and arrived at work an hour late.
He was so engrossed in solving the equation that he failed to notice the bell, and the classroom emptied around him.

mesmerize.definition: to hold someone's attention so completely that they seem entranced
sentences: The swirling patterns of the fireworks seemed to mesmerize the crowd, which stood in silent wonder long after the display had ended.
Her hypnotic voice mesmerized listeners, and many of them later admitted that they could not recall anything but its soft, steady rhythm.
mesmerize.mnemonic: Du nom de Mesmer, médecin qui hypnotisait ses patients.

transfix.definition: to render motionless with awe, terror or amazement
sentences: The sight of the enormous bear emerging from the trees seemed to transfix the hikers, who stood frozen and unable to flee.
The magician's final trick transfixed the audience, holding every eye on the stage until the curtain finally came down.
transfix.mnemonic: Trans + fix : fixé sur place, immobile.

sentences: The lawyer presented such compelling evidence of the defendant's innocence that the jury needed less than an hour to acquit him.
The memoir is compelling reading, for its author describes her escape from war with a honesty that few readers can ignore.

staggering.definition: astonishing because of enormous size or amount
sentences: The company reported staggering losses of several billion dollars, a sum so large that analysts struggled to explain how it had accumulated.
Archaeologists were amazed by the staggering scale of the buried city, which stretched across an area far larger than they had imagined.

dazzle.definition: to amaze or overwhelm with brilliant display, or blind with bright light
sentences: The dancer's flawless technique and dramatic costumes were meant to dazzle the judges, who had seen hundreds of ordinary performances that week.
Headlights from the oncoming truck dazzled the driver, who braked sharply and squinted until his vision gradually returned to normal.

enticing.definition: attractive and tempting, drawing people in
sentences: The aroma of fresh bread drifting from the bakery was so enticing that few passersby could resist stepping inside for a loaf.
The company offered enticing bonuses to attract talented engineers, hoping that the promise of generous rewards would persuade them to leave their rivals.

palatable.definition: pleasant to taste; or acceptable and satisfactory to the mind
sentences: The chef added a little sugar to make the bitter sauce more palatable, and even the fussiest guests cleaned their plates.
To make the unpopular budget palatable to voters, the minister emphasized its benefits for schools and softened its most controversial tax increases.
palatable.mnemonic: Palatable : palais (du goût) ; ce qui plaît au palais.

relish.definition: to enjoy greatly and take keen pleasure in
sentences: After months of hard work, she began to relish every quiet morning on her porch, sipping coffee and watching the sun rise.
The old professor did not relish the prospect of retirement, for he had always loved lecturing and debating with eager students.

revel.definition: to take great delight in; to celebrate noisily
revel.definitionFr: se délecter de ; faire la fête
sentences: The villagers gathered in the square to revel in their team's victory, singing and dancing through the night until sunrise.
He seemed to revel in the controversy surrounding his book, giving interview after interview and clearly enjoying every moment of the debate.

fleeting.definition: lasting for only a very short time
sentences: She caught only a fleeting glimpse of the rare bird before it vanished into the dense forest canopy above her.
Fame in the music industry is often fleeting, since a song that tops the charts one summer is usually forgotten by the next.

wane.definition: to decrease gradually in strength, size or influence
sentences: As the evening wore on, the crowd's enthusiasm began to wane, and by midnight only a handful of fans remained in the stadium.
Once the most powerful empire in the region, the kingdom saw its influence wane steadily as rivals grew richer and better armed.
wane.mnemonic: Wane (déclin de la lune) s'oppose à wax (croissant).

dwindle.definition: to become gradually smaller, fewer or weaker
sentences: As the drought continued, the village's supply of fresh water began to dwindle, and families were forced to ration every drop.
Public support for the policy dwindled over the following months, until only a small group of loyal activists still defended it.

fledgling.definition: new and inexperienced, just starting to develop
sentences: The fledgling company struggled in its first year, lacking both the capital and the experience needed to compete with established rivals.
Mentors helped the fledgling democracy establish courts and elections, though many of its institutions remained fragile and untested in their early years.
fledgling.mnemonic: Fledgling = oisillon qui vient d'avoir ses plumes, encore maladroit.

tyro.definition: a beginner with no experience in a skill or field
sentences: Although the veteran chess master crushed the tyro in only a dozen moves, he kindly explained each of the beginner's mistakes afterward.
As a tyro in the laboratory, the first-year student needed constant supervision, since she had never before handled any of the delicate instruments.
tyro.mnemonic: Tyro ~ « tiro » : le tirailleur novice latin (tiro).

trailblazer.definition: a person who makes a new path, pioneering something that others later follow
sentences: As the first woman to lead a major research university, she was a trailblazer who opened doors for countless female scholars after her.
The engineer was a trailblazer in renewable energy, building working solar plants decades before other companies took the technology seriously.

groundbreaking.definition: pioneering and innovative, introducing completely new methods or ideas
sentences: The scientist's groundbreaking discovery of the new particle transformed physics, forcing researchers to rewrite textbooks that had stood for fifty years.
Critics hailed the director's groundbreaking film for its original techniques, which no studio had ever attempted before and which many later imitated.

maverick.definition: an independent person who refuses to conform to the views of a group
sentences: The senator, a maverick who often voted against his own party, earned admiration from voters who valued independence over loyalty.
As a maverick in the fashion world, the designer ignored seasonal trends and produced bold collections that no other label would have dared to show.
maverick.mnemonic: Maverick : veau sans marque du Texan Maverick, qui échappe au troupeau.

herald.definition: to announce, or to be a sign that something is coming
sentences: Trumpets sounded to herald the arrival of the king, and the crowd along the road fell silent and bowed their heads.
Many economists believe that the new invention will herald a revolution in manufacturing, changing how goods are made throughout the world.

harbinger.definition: a person or thing that signals the approach of something
sentences: The first robin of the year is often called a harbinger of spring, since it appears just as the snow begins to melt.
Analysts viewed the sudden bank failure as a harbinger of wider financial trouble, and they warned that other institutions might soon collapse.

portend.definition: to be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, will happen
sentences: Dark clouds gathering over the harbor seemed to portend a violent storm, and the fishermen hurried to secure their boats.
Many historians argue that the rising unrest in the capital portended the collapse of the regime, though few contemporaries recognized the danger.

foreseeable.definition: able to be predicted or expected in advance
sentences: The accident was entirely foreseeable, since engineers had warned for years that the aging bridge could not bear the weight of modern traffic.
Because the company expects steady demand for the foreseeable future, its managers have decided against any further reductions in staff.

impending.definition: about to happen, especially of something threatening
sentences: Residents of the coast were warned of the impending hurricane and urged to leave their homes before the first heavy winds arrived.
The student felt anxious about the impending exam, which loomed only two days away and covered material she had barely begun to review.

beget.definition: to cause or bring about, as a result; to father
sentences: Historians often say that violence begets violence, since each act of revenge provokes a new response and prolongs the cycle of conflict.
Poverty can beget poor health, which in turn begets further poverty, creating a cycle that is extremely difficult for families to escape.

spawn.definition: to give rise to or produce in large numbers
sentences: The success of the original film went on to spawn a dozen sequels, each of which copied its formula with less and less originality.
Rapid industrialization tended to spawn crowded slums at the edges of cities, as thousands of workers arrived with nowhere affordable to live.

foster.definition: to encourage the development or growth of something
sentences: The teacher tried to foster a love of reading by letting students choose their own books and discuss them in small groups.
Government grants were intended to foster innovation in small businesses, giving young entrepreneurs the resources they needed to test bold ideas.

coalesce.definition: to come together and form a single whole
sentences: Over several months, scattered protests across the country began to coalesce into a single organized movement with a clear set of demands.
As the oil droplets coalesced on the surface of the water, they formed larger pools that eventually separated entirely from the liquid below.

suffuse.definition: to spread over or through, gradually filling with color, light or feeling
sentences: The setting sun seemed to suffuse the valley with a warm golden glow, and every hillside looked as if it were lit from within.
A sense of quiet joy suffused the room as the family gathered around the table, and all their earlier quarrels were forgotten.

imbue.definition: to fill thoroughly with a quality, feeling or value
sentences: Her grandmother worked hard to imbue the children with a respect for education, reading to them each night and praising every small achievement.
The sculptor imbued the marble figure with such emotion that visitors often felt the statue was about to speak or begin moving.

pervasive.definition: spreading widely and present throughout every part of something
sentences: Smartphones have become so pervasive that it is now unusual to see a commuter on a train who is not staring at a screen.
The pervasive smell of smoke filled every room of the house, and no amount of open windows could remove it entirely.

bolster.definition: to support, strengthen or boost something
sentences: The new data helped bolster the researchers' hypothesis, giving skeptical colleagues a strong reason to take their controversial theory more seriously.
The central bank cut interest rates to bolster the struggling economy, hoping that cheaper loans would encourage businesses to hire and invest.
bolster.mnemonic: Bolster = traversin (coussin) : il soutient la tête.

buttress.definition: to support or strengthen an argument or structure
sentences: The lawyer cited three recent studies to buttress her claim, hoping the statistics would convince the skeptical jury of her client's innocence.
Workers added stone supports to buttress the crumbling wall of the cathedral, which had begun leaning dangerously toward the street.
buttress.mnemonic: Buttress : arc-boutant, le contrefort des cathédrales.

underscore.definition: to emphasize or highlight the importance of something
sentences: The recent earthquake serves to underscore the importance of strict building codes, which saved many lives in the better constructed districts.
In her closing remarks, the speaker underscored the urgency of the climate crisis, repeating that further delay would make the damage irreversible.

substantiate.definition: to provide evidence that proves a claim to be true
sentences: The journalist could not substantiate the rumor, since no witness would speak openly and no document supported the shocking allegation.
Scientists must substantiate their claims with repeatable experiments before the wider community will accept a surprising new theory as fact.

uphold.definition: to confirm or maintain, especially a decision, law or principle
sentences: The appeals court voted to uphold the original verdict, rejecting the defense argument that the trial had been conducted unfairly.
A good judge must uphold the law even when it conflicts with personal opinion or the shifting demands of popular sentiment.

mainstay.definition: a person or thing that is the chief support of something
sentences: Agriculture has long been the mainstay of the local economy, employing most residents and supplying nearly all of the region's exports.
The veteran goalkeeper was the mainstay of the team for a decade, and the club struggled badly after he retired.

credence.definition: acceptance of something as true or believable
sentences: The discovery of the ancient letter lends credence to the legend, which most historians had previously dismissed as pure invention.
Few scientists give credence to the claim, since no laboratory has ever managed to reproduce the supposed result.

undermine.definition: to weaken gradually, especially by secretly damaging the foundations of something
sentences: Constant rumors and gossip began to undermine the manager's authority, until even her closest allies doubted that she could lead the team.
Critics argued that the new law would undermine public trust in the courts by allowing wealthy defendants to buy favorable treatment.

undercut.definition: to weaken the effect of; or to sell at a lower price than a competitor
sentences: The small airline managed to undercut its larger rivals by charging far lower fares, and within a year it had captured much of the market.
Her sarcastic comment undercut the seriousness of the speech, and the audience, which had been listening attentively, began to laugh.
